rss.title: Open-source AI without Jensen
rss.summary: A decapitation. It’s time to rebuild.
rss.text_excerpt:
The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on. Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up. In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ( slides , recording ). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside. The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is. The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy . Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jens

rss.summary: Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3 OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header . Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy. datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. rss.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
rss.summary: ArtCraft used AI to rewrite Photoshop as open source software. For CEO Brandon Thomas, the vision is even bigger: to take back the internet!
rss.text_excerpt:
The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI . And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools , starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft . You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting billed with an unexpected fee when he cancelled a monthly plan. “It's really frustrating that the web — that was once really, really promising and open and free — has turned into this extractive, owned, rent-seeking world.” This inspired him to start ArtCraft, “with the ethos of ‘let's build everything open source.’” A message even anti-AI people have gotten behind, according to Thomas. Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM during Web 2.0, but in the AI era it does actually signify a harsh reality about LLM-driven software: sometimes it’s just not very smart. > An agentic runtime for system programmers - in Ruby. The runtime supports concurrent and parallel tool execution. 15+ providers. Parallel execution is provided by Ractor, and the fork system call. Concurrent execution is provided by Thread, Fiber, and the 'async' gem (optional). Works with ActiveRecord, and Sequel. Works with and without Rails. It requires nothing but Ruby's standard library. It can be extended with optional, opt-in dependencies. ## Install ##### v17 The v17 series requires Ruby 3.4 or later.
This version works with older rubies and dependencies (ie: json v2). ```bash gem install llm.rb -v 17.0.1 ``` ##### Latest (v21) v21 is the recommended release. The v19 release is a smaller release that includes a tiny eval framework that was authored for the [micro1](https://micro1.ai) hackathon. v18 includes [substational runtime improvements](changelog/v18.md) - especially for running tool calls on a [Ractor](https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/4.0/Ractor.html). Requires Ruby4+, JSON v3, and the latest versions of ActiveRecord|Sequel (optional). ```bash gem install llm.rb ``` ## Quick start ### Resources [r.uby.dev](https://r.uby.dev) is the place to go if you have a question the README doesn't answer or want to see the runtime in action. Great way to learn about the runtime and see it in action at the same time. [API docs](https://r.uby.dev/api-docs/llm.rb/) also exists for people who prefer learning the traditional way. For everything else, there's the README. ### Agents The [`LLM::Agent`](https://r.uby.dev/api-docs/llm.rb/LLM/Agent.html) class is the default high-level interface, and it is recommended for most use-cases. It manages the tool loop and provides configurable features on top of it. For example you can manage the tool loop with a retry budget and a tool call budget - alongside other features. # hf-to-litertlm Convert open-weight Hugging Face LLMs and VLMs into `.litertlm` bundles for Google's LiteRT-LM runtime (Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux). There are 116 published conversions below, most with speeds measured on a phone and a Mac.

If you want an open model in an Android or iPhone app, look for it in the [list of converted models](#converted-models) first. If it isn't there, [ask for it](https://github.com/john-rocky/hf-to-litertlm/issues/new?template=model-request.yml) with the model's Hugging Face link. I reply on the issue with the bundle, the recipe and the measured numbers, or the reason it couldn't be converted. Two SDKs already load these files by repo name: [react-native-litert-lm](https://github.com/hung-yueh/react-native-litert-lm) and [flutter_edge_ai](https://github.com/DenisovAV/flutter_edge_ai). ## Try a published model On a Mac, before it goes on a phone (needs [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)): ```bash uvx litert-lm@0.18.0 run \ --from-huggingface-repo=litert-community/LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct \ LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct_int4_gpu.litertlm \ --prompt="What is 17 + 25? Answer briefly." ``` To use a published bundle in an Android app, add [hfmodels-android](https://github.com/john-rocky/hfmodels-android) with one Gradle dependency and a few lines of Kotlin ([code](docs/apps.md#android)). In an iPhone app, it loads through [swift-litert-lm](https://github.com/john-rocky/swift-litert-lm) ([code](docs/apps.md#iphone)). ## Convert a finetune ```bash uvx hf-to-litertlm / ``` That runs `convert.py` from PyPI and writes the bundle under `./out`. Read its README and CLI help, install Daydream with uv and Python 3.14+, and help me authenticate a supported backend (Claude by default, or Codex or Pi). Run a report-only review with --review against the intended base branch. Show me the findings and where the trajectory was saved. ``` Daydream reviews code changes, can fix findings and run tests, and records [ATIF](https://www.harborframework.com/docs/agents/trajectory-format) trajectories for research toward an open-weight code-review model. Its review quality is measured in public on AACR-Bench and ReviewBench in [code-review-benchmarks](https://github.com/existential-birds/code-review-benchmarks). ## Quick start Requires [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), Python 3.14+, and an authenticated [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code) CLI (default backend), or Codex or Pi. Osprey cannot run a review. PR comments also require authenticated [gh](https://cli.github.com/). ```bash git clone https://github.com/existential-birds/daydream.git cd daydream uv tool install --editable . # If daydream is missing from PATH: uv tool update-shell, then restart your shell. ``` ## Review code ```bash daydream /path/to/project # report only (same as --review) daydream --comment /path/to/project # post inline PR comments daydream --fix /path/to/project # review, offer fixes, test, commit and push daydream --review --backend codex --base main /path/to/project ``` A review ends with findings; only `--fix` [selects fixing](docs/runtime.md#validation-and-repair), and `--yes` answers its gates. One reviewer covers the whole change and challenges every finding in a fresh context before reporting it; it needs a backend with native host tools (Pi, Claude or Codex). Use `--help` for common options and `--help-all` for configuration and advanced flags. Reports land in `.review-output.md`; trajectories in `.daydream/runs/<id>/`.
